content.text:
Checked all four. Two of your premises hold, one breaks, and one has a hidden conflict.

## The conflict: token-stripping fights the rewrite

We established `filepath` must equal the markdown token, because `pathMapping` is keyed on it and `updateMarkdownAssetLinks` does the lookup. The normalizer is minimal:

```js
// importNodes.ts:507
p.replace(/^\.\//, "").replace(/\/+/g, "/").trim()
```

Strips `./`, collapses slashes. **Nothing about query strings.** So a tokenless `filepath` will not match a tokened URL in the markdown — the rewrite silently finds nothing and the link stays pointing at Firebase. Either keep the token in `filepath`, or teach both sides to normalize by stripping the query before lookup. Can't just drop it.

## And the security gain may be zero — it depends on the pivot

Under reading **(A)** (markdown keeps its Firebase URLs), the tokened URL sits in `Content.text` verbatim — it has to, for the fallback path and for Roam→Roam rendering. Stripping the token from `filepath` then protects nothing: it's in the same database, one column over. You'd pay the metadata cost for no boundary.

Under **(B)** it would be a genuine boundary.

So this isn't an independent decision — it's **downstream of the A/B pivot**. Worth not settling it before that.

## Your collision premise is wrong for this code path

I read it. There's no disambiguation:

```
targetPath = overwritePath ?? `${importBasePath}/${sanitizedAssetPath}`
  exists? -> compare mtimes -> skip, or OVERWRITE
```

No `-1` suffix, no rename. Same-hash reuse is handled (via `importedAssets[filehash]`), but **two different assets whose names sanitize to the same target path clobber each other**, silently, with an mtime check as the only gate. Obsidian-the-app disambiguates user attachment drops; this importer doesn't. So collisions are data loss, not cosmetic — which pushes hard toward your collision-free option.

## The options

| | network | collides | readable | breaks match |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Firebase `metadata["file-name"]`** | 1 fetch/asset | **yes → clobber** | yes | no |
| **10-char id from URL** | none | no | no | no |
| **fake query param** | none | no | yes | **yes** |
| **filename in markdown link text** | 1 fetch at publish | yes → clobber | yes | no |

**Fake query param is the worst of these** — beyond fragility, it mutates the URL string, which re-breaks the markdown match, and it hides a private encoding inside a primary-key column where a stray `&name=` could meet a real Firebase param.

**The id option is stronger than "looks like nothing."** `lqp2ioVNC3.png` is derivable from the URL by pure string work — no Firebase round trip at publish *or* import, which also removes a dependency on an undocumented descriptor endpoint. Uniqueness is per-graph (`imgs/app/<graphName>/<name>`), and `importBasePath` already includes the space name, so cross-space collisions stay contained.

## One option you didn't list

Put the filename in the **markdown link text at publish time** — `[CleanShot 2025-11-16.png](url)`. The design already invented exactly this device for the opposite direction: ENG-2217's "Label a non-media link with the source filename, so the reader sees `[report.docx](url)`." Roam publish holds the token anyway, does one cheap descriptor read, and the human name then travels inside `Content.text` — no schema change, no import-time fetch, and it degrades gracefully since it's just link text.

It doesn't solve collisions on its own. But **combined with the id as the vault filename** you get both: `lqp2ioVNC3.png` on disk (safe, unique), the real name visible in the note body.

That'd be my recommendation — id for the path, name in link text — with the token question deferred until A/B is settled, since that's what decides whether stripping it buys anything.

content.text:
Correct, and worse than that when I check it against the actual Roam embed shapes.

Your objection is the ordinary case: `[my figure 3](url)` — writing the filename over the author's caption destroys real content, and if we only write into *empty* slots, then Obsidian can no longer tell "this text is a filename we placed" from "this is the author's caption." An untrustworthy signal is worse than no signal, because the importer has to guess.

But the structural problem is bigger. Per the design's own inventory of `file.upload` return shapes:

```
images        ![](url)              text slot, often empty, may be occupied
pdf           {{[[pdf]]: url}}      NO text slot
audio         {{[[audio]]: url}}    NO text slot
video         {{[[video]]: url}}    NO text slot
everything    <bare url>            NO text slot
```

Three of five shapes have nowhere to put it, and the bare-URL case has nowhere either. So the device is available **only for images**, and only for images whose alt text is empty — which is precisely the case where the filename matters least, since the thing renders inline and nobody reads the name. For a PDF or a `.docx`, where a vault file called `GVfB6XBcMR.pdf` is genuinely bad, the slot doesn't exist at all.

So: withdrawn. It inverts — available where it's useless, absent where it's needed.

That leaves the honest position:

**v0 uses the id from the URL.** Deterministic, collision-free, zero network calls at either end, no dependency on an undocumented descriptor endpoint. The original filename is simply not carried. Worth noting Roam itself accepts this outcome — `file.get` falls back to the storage uid when `metadata["file-name"]` is absent, which is why their own docs show `File {name: "GVfB6XBcMR.pdf"}`.

**Post-v0, the filename rides along with the rename you already proposed.** When `filepath` becomes `source_ref`, add a nullable `display_name` beside it. That's one migration doing two related jobs, and it's the only place the name can live where a consumer can actually trust it. The publisher fills it from `metadata["file-name"]` when the descriptor read succeeds, leaves it null otherwise, and Obsidian falls back to the id — which is exactly the degradation behavior the importer already needs for the URL-only case.

Which also means: the Firebase descriptor read stops being load-bearing for v0 entirely. It moves from "how we get the filename" to "an optimization we can add later," and the metadata finding in Context becomes background rather than a dependency.

The collision-clobber in `importNodes.ts` is worth its own ticket regardless of any of this — it's a pre-existing data-loss path that our new asset volume will make more likely, not one this change introduces.

Back to A/B whenever you want it.

content.text:
Checked the trigger, and it matters for your question: the landmine D1 identified is **entirely about `filehash` being nullable**, not about extra columns.

```sql
PERFORM pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext(OLD.filehash));
IF NOT public.file_exists(OLD.filehash) THEN
    INSERT INTO public.file_gc VALUES (OLD.filehash);   -- NULL lands here
```

So the two changes are not the same change:

| | triggers | GC | `file_access` | D1's verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (i) add nullable `url`, keep `filehash NOT NULL` | untouched | untouched | untouched | **never actually evaluated** |
| (ii) make `filehash` nullable so URL-only refs become rows | breaks | changes | — | rejected, correctly |

D1 rejected the pair as a bundle, because it wanted URL-only rows. You've since agreed a URL-only fallback isn't a reference at all — so (ii) is off the table on its own merits, and (i) inherits none of that rejection. Worth stating explicitly in the decision, because "D1 already said no to a `url` column" is the objection someone will raise, and it isn't true of what you're proposing.

## B is what justifies it, and it retires your own earlier argument

Your one-column reasoning was "there is no case where we'd have both a URL and a filepath." That held under A. **Under B it's false.** B means Roam publish rewrites its markdown to a stable reference the way Obsidian does — so a Roam-origin asset has a synthesized reference token *and* a Firebase origin URL, simultaneously. Two facts, two columns. That's not scope creep dressed up; it's B making a second fact exist.

And there's a real consumer, not just provenance. Under B without `url`, a **Roam→Roam** import goes: download from Supabase → re-upload to Firebase → brand-new duplicate blob, burning the user's Roam quota. With `url` stored, the importer just reuses the original Firebase URL — no upload, no duplicate, no registry entry. That's D4's dedup goal achieved for free on that path. Plus re-fetch if a Supabase copy is ever lost, which is the durability property D3 spent its whole argument on.

## What B dissolves

Most of the last hour resolves itself, which is worth naming:

- `filepath` stops being a URL, so the `split("/").map(sanitizeFileName)` breakage **goes away** — the token is path-shaped again.
- The token-stripping question goes away as a `filepath` concern. It reappears as "what do we store in `url`," where the answer is obviously *the whole thing*, since it's provenance, not a key.
- The id-vs-filename choice stays, but becomes low-stakes: `filepath` holds whatever name we synthesize, and if you're already migrating, a nullable `display_name` alongside `url` is one migration doing all three jobs.

## The honest counterweight

"Avoid scope changes" cuts both ways here. B is *less* deviation from the Obsidian pattern and *more* implementation than A: Roam publish gains a link-rewriting stage it doesn't have today, and B **breaks the ENG-1872 narrowing** — Roam-origin markdown no longer carries a world-readable URL, so ENG-2217's `http`/`https` pass-through stops being sufficient and ENG-2219's copy stage has to handle both origins. That's the note I wrote this morning and the tickets that quote it.

So the schema change is the cheap part. Re-planning the split is the expensive part, and it's implied by B whether or not you add the column.

Want me to work through what B does to the four sub-issues?

content.text:
Let me re-check that claim rather than restate it, because I think I under-weighted one thing.

**Where I was right:** the data isn't lost. You kept the token in `filepath`, so the descriptor read stays available — postponing `filename` is backfillable at any time from the URL you already store. That's a real asymmetry worth naming: if you postponed **`url`** under B you'd lose provenance permanently once markdown was rewritten; postponing **`filename`** loses nothing recoverable.

**Where I was too glib:** the DB backfill being easy doesn't make the postponement free, because of what happens in the vault in the meantime.

```
ship without filename  ->  user imports  ->  vault gets  lqp2ioVNC3.png
                       ->  user links it in their own notes
                       ->  add filename column later, backfill fine
                       ->  but renaming the vault file now breaks THEIR links
```

So the cost isn't in the database, it's one-way and user-facing. Files already imported keep their opaque names essentially forever, because renaming them later breaks links the user wrote themselves. It's the same escape-hatch problem D6 identified for deletion: once a reference leaves our bookkeeping, we can't touch the file.

That reframes the question. It isn't "now vs. later," it's **"before or after Roam→Obsidian asset import reaches real vaults."** If those ship together, postponing costs nothing at all. If Roam-origin assets land in vaults first, you're accepting permanent debris in exchange for a migration you're going to run anyway.

Three things that shrink the decision further:

- **Technically it's trivial and safe.** A nullable `filename` touches no trigger, no PK, no RLS, no GC path — same clean bill as the `url` analysis. The cost of adding it now is one column plus populating it at publish time. The expense is process (a scope change on the ticket), not engineering.
- **It's Roam-origin-only.** Obsidian-origin `filepath` is a vault path that already contains the name, so the column is derivable-or-redundant on that side. That genuinely weakens "add it now" — it serves one direction.
- **Absence is already a known case, not a hypothetical.** design.md records that Roam's own `file.get` falls back to the storage uid when `metadata["file-name"]` is missing. So the importer needs the id fallback regardless; `filename` is an enhancement over a path that must exist anyway. That's an argument for postponing — nothing is *blocked* on it.

Net: I'd say **low cost to postpone, conditional on sequencing.** Add it now only if Roam-origin assets will reach users' vaults before you'd otherwise run the rename migration. Otherwise fold `filepath` → `path_or_url` and `+ filename` into one migration later, and let v0 use the id with the fallback the importer needs anyway.

The one thing I'd not postpone is deciding the id derivation rule and writing it down, since that's what determines the names users get stuck with.

content.text:
That's the decisive argument, and it changes my answer.

The concrete shape of postponing is a line in Obsidian's importer that reads roughly:

```ts
if (filepath.startsWith("https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/")) {
  // strip alt=media, fetch descriptor, read metadata["file-name"], which is Roam's own key
}
```

That's origin detection by string shape, in the destination, load-bearing. It's precisely the coupling the FileReference contract exists to prevent — and it puts *Roam* knowledge inside the *Obsidian* plugin, where nobody will think to update it when Roam changes.

With the column, the importer's rule is origin-free: **use `filename` if present, else derive from `filepath`.** Roam-origin and Obsidian-origin take the identical path. The origin-specific work — knowing about Firebase descriptors and Roam's metadata key — lives in the Roam publisher, which is already Roam-specific by definition and already holds the tokened URL. That's the right side of the boundary.

Two things fall out that I hadn't weighted:

**It also fixes the `split("/")` breakage.** If the vault name comes from `filename` when present, a Roam-origin row never reaches `getAssetPathRelativeToNote` and `.split("/").map(sanitizeFileName)`. The URL stays purely a `pathMapping` key and is never treated as a path. So `filename` isn't only cosmetic — it's what makes URL-shaped `filepath` safe at all. Without it you need the origin-sniffing branch *anyway*, just for the path derivation, so postponing doesn't even avoid the branch.

**The descriptor read moves from N×M to N.** Once per asset at publish, instead of once per asset per importing vault.

So I'd revise to: **add `filename` now.** Not for readability — for the boundary. It's the column that lets the destination stay origin-agnostic, and it converts a fragile cross-plugin dependency into a value the publisher writes once.

One honest caveat, since it argues for sequencing rather than against the column: filenames aren't unique, so using `filename` as the vault name walks into the clobber path in `importNodes.ts` — overwrite with an mtime check, no disambiguation. It doesn't *introduce* that risk (Obsidian-origin vault paths can already collide after sanitization), but it does widen the mouth of it. That makes the collision ticket a real prerequisite rather than the nice-to-have I filed it as two turns ago.

And your earlier PK objection is fully respected here: `filename` is a plain nullable attribute, not part of `(source_local_id, space_id, filepath)`. Uniqueness is still carried by the URL.

content.text:
You're right, and it's worth stating precisely because it changes what the collision ticket is *for*.

**Before:** `filepath` is a vault path. Paths are unique within a vault by construction, and the target is `import/{spaceName}/…`, so uniqueness is inherited. Nothing to collide.

One narrow exception, which is the only pre-existing exposure: `getAssetPathRelativeToNote` strips the note's directory when the asset sits under it. So `notes/foo/img.png` (note `notes/foo/note.md`) and `notes/bar/img.png` (note `notes/bar/note.md`) both relativize to `img.png` and land on `import/{space}/img.png`. Real, but it takes two notes each keeping a same-named asset beside them. Plus the theoretical case of `sanitizeFileName` mapping two distinct paths onto one. Both narrow.

**After:** `filename` is a leaf name, not a path — and Roam has no asset hierarchy at all. Every upload in a graph lands flat at `imgs/app/<graphName>/<random>.<ext>`, so the only thing distinguishing two assets is a name a human typed. In practice that means `image.png`, `Screenshot.png`, `Pasted image.png`, repeatedly.

```
Obsidian-origin   notes/foo/diagram.png   hierarchical, unique by construction
Roam-origin       image.png               flat, no uniqueness guarantee at all
```

So the change doesn't widen an existing exposure — I had that wrong. It **replaces a structurally-unique key with a non-unique one**, and then feeds it to a code path whose collision behavior is "overwrite if the mtime check allows." Two different screenshots both pasted as `image.png` into two Roam nodes, published, imported into one space: one silently overwrites the other.

That reframes the prerequisite. It isn't "fix a latent bug that's now more likely" — it's **the disambiguation is part of this feature**, because the feature is what introduces the flat namespace. Standard fix, and what Obsidian-the-app already does for user attachment drops: suffix on conflict, `image.png` / `image-1.png`, keyed off the hash so re-imports stay stable.

Worth adding to the proposal's Triage reason, or keeping as a linked prerequisite ticket? It's a one-line addition either way — something like "importer must disambiguate colliding filenames; Roam's asset namespace is flat" — but it does change the size of the work the proposal implies, so burying it would misrepresent the cost.

content.content: ## Goals / Non-Goals **Goals:** - One asset-reference shape both directions can be described in, so the four follow-up tickets stop at implementation rather than re-deciding the payload. - Never fail a node import or a node publish because of an asset. Every asset failure degrades to the link already in the markdown, and is reported. - Choose deliberately between revocable and durable for mirrored bytes, and record why — this is the decision most likely to be revisited. **Non-Goals:** - Not an asset synchronization system. There is no refresh when upstream bytes change, and no deletion. - Not an access-control mechanism. Nothing here narrows or widens who can see an asset; visibility follows the referencing node's existing row-level security, or, once mirrored, follows Firebase. - Not a general blob store abstraction. Two hosts, two storage models, one narrow bridge. ## Decisions ### 1. Find assets by parsing markdown; store no asset index - Asset references are discovered by parsing the `full` markdown content of a node. No new rows record which node references which asset, and `FileReference` is not extended. - **Why:** every candidate column turned out to have no reader. A reference token is already present in the markdown, and every consumer has to parse that markdown anyway in order to rewrite links — so an index would be a second copy of information nobody reads from the copy. Recording Roam-origin Firebase URLs as rows would be write-only data: we cannot revoke those bytes, cannot garbage-collect them, and cannot serve them, so nothing would ever query the row. A work list for the deferred "pull Roam assets into Supabase" future is derivable at any time with a regex over `Content.text` where `variant = 'full'`. **Alternatives considered:** - **Make `filehash` nullable and add a `url` column**, so a `FileReference` can point at bytes we deliberately never store. Rejected: no consumer, per above. It also requires guarding both trigger functions in `supabase/schemas/assets.sql` — `after_delete_update_fref` would otherwise reach `INSERT INTO public.file_gc VALUES (NULL)` on any delete of a NULL-hash row, since `file_exists(NULL)` is false, and fail the delete outright. And the deferred transfer future does not need it either: downloading a Firebase asset and calling `addFile` produces an ordinary hashed row. - **Add `mimetype` and `size` columns**, backfilled from `storage.objects.metadata`. Rejected once the Vercel route (Decision 3) was set aside: the mirror path downloads the blob anyway and gets `.type` and `.size` from the response for free. Note the argument deliberately does **not** rest on Obsidian's current 6 MB publish cap (`syncDgNodesToSupabase.ts:706`), which is expected to rise — a pre-flight size check becomes worth having once large files can reach the bucket, but `storage.objects.metadata` already carries size and is readable through the storage API, so the answer is still a metadata read rather than a column. **Accepted cost:** asset enumeration requires markdown parsing, which is more expensive and less precise than a table lookup. Acceptable for v0; if a consumer ever needs enumeration without parsing, the nullable-`filehash`-plus-`url` shape above is the design to revive. ### 2. Roam-origin assets stay on Firebase - Roam publishes its markdown with Firebase URLs intact. Nothing is transferred to Supabase, and no `FileReference` is written for them. - **Why:** the [Roam decision note](https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/3dI5iyDAI) accepted that these URLs leak. Given that, copying the bytes buys nothing a destination cannot already do by following the link. - This direction is therefore nearly free, and it is free for every destination, not just Obsidian. An Obsidian import of a Roam-origin node leaves the URL alone (`importNodes.ts:643`) and the image renders from the web. A Roam-to-Roam import is the same case: the URL passes through the importer's `http`/`https` rule untouched, and the second graph renders it by following the link. **No code branches on origin** — the pass-through rule is what makes Roam-origin assets work, which is why ENG-1872 could narrow to Obsidian-origin without leaving a gap. ENG-1870 reduces to detecting and reporting; ENG-1873 reduces to confirming the existing behavior. ### 3. Mirror Obsidian-origin assets to Firebase, choosing durability over revocability - At import time the Roam client downloads the asset from the Supabase bucket with its authenticated client and re-uploads it via `file.upload`, then rewrites the markdown link to the returned URL. - **Why:** Roam renders `![](url)` as an ``, which issues an **anonymous cross-origin GET** — no `Authorization` header, and cookies are third-party. content.text:
You're right, and that's a cleaner reading of the principle than mine — agnosticism applies to *both* destinations, not just Obsidian. I carved out a Roam-side exception on efficiency grounds, which reintroduces exactly the origin-branching we added `filename` to eliminate.

One thing that makes it less unfortunate than it looks: **the round trip buys durability, not just consistency.** Pass-through leaves graph B's page pointing at graph A's Firebase blob — so if A's owner deletes that upload, B's image silently stops rendering, and nothing in our bookkeeping can see it. Copying severs that. It's the same durable-over-revocable trade D3 already made deliberately. And D4's registry means it's one round trip per asset *per graph*, not per import — a second node referencing the same asset short-circuits on the hash.

But this does undo more of this morning than my last message implied:

**ENG-2217's rule changes substantively, not just its Notes.** "Leave `http`/`https` links unchanged" is wrong as a blanket rule — it would pass a Roam-origin URL straight through instead of resolving it. The rule has to become:

> Resolve a reference through its `FileReference` row when one matches the token. Leave it unchanged only when no row matches.

Which is origin-agnostic and still handles genuinely external links (`example.com` has no row) and the broken/URL-only case you did agree to. That's a Solution-line change plus a Done When line.

**ENG-1872's narrowing is wrong after all.** If the import path resolves by row regardless of origin, then it isn't Obsidian-origin work — it's just asset import. The title I changed this morning ("Copy **Obsidian-origin** assets into Roam on import") should go back to something origin-neutral, close to its original "Import and preserve shared assets in Roam materialization." And the whole Roam-origin justification note we've been revising gets **deleted**, not rewritten — there's nothing left to justify.

**And `design.md` D2 is now wrong where I just wrote it.** Its "Why the URL stays in the markdown" cites the Roam-to-Roam pass-through as a reason. That's no longer a reason. The other three hold — PK component, `pathMapping` key, and the degradation path when no row exists — so the bullet needs the pass-through clause struck and the fallback framing kept. D3 also needs to say the mirror now serves both origins.

So the revised set is:

| | change |
|---|---|
| `design.md` D2 | strike the pass-through justification, keep the other three |
| `design.md` D3 | mirror serves both origins; note the round trip and why it's accepted |
| ENG-1872 | retitle origin-neutral; **delete** the Roam-origin note |
| ENG-2217 | Solution + Done When: resolve by row, pass through only when no row |
| ENG-2219 | copy stage is origin-agnostic — check its wording |

content.text:
Design edits applied. Packet regenerated (cumulative, diff + per-block text): `…/scratchpad/design-B-mirror-packet.md`

D3 also got retitled — "Mirror **Obsidian-origin** assets to Firebase" → "**Mirror assets into Firebase on import**", since it's no longer origin-specific.

---

# Proposed Linear revisions

## ENG-1872

**Title:** `Copy Obsidian-origin assets into Roam on import` → **`Copy shared assets into Roam on import`**

**Problem**, bullet 1 — currently opens "Obsidian attachments live in a private Supabase bucket." Replace:
> Shared assets live in a private Supabase bucket. A browser cannot fetch them without credentials, and Roam embeds a file only by URL, so images in an imported node do not render. This holds whatever the asset's origin: a Roam-origin asset is in that same bucket, because publish put it there.

**Solution**, bullet 1:
> Copy each asset referenced by the node into Roam storage during materialization, resolving it through its `FileReference` row regardless of origin.

**Notes** — **delete** the Roam-origin bullet entirely. Replace with:
> This ticket does not branch on origin, and must not. A Roam-origin asset imported into a second Roam graph travels Firebase → Supabase → Firebase and lands as a fresh blob. That round trip is deliberate — see [Decision 3](https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/CnYTDCLp_). Skipping it would require the importer to recognise a Firebase URL, which is exactly the origin-detection [Decision 8] removes, and would leave this graph's page depending on a blob the origin graph's owner can delete.

## ENG-2217

**Solution** — replace `Leave `http` and `https` links unchanged` with:
> Resolve each reference through its `FileReference` row when one matches the token. Leave a token unchanged only when no row matches.

**Done When** — replace the external-URL line:
> A node referencing an image, a PDF, and an external URL produces correct Roam syntax for the two assets and leaves the external URL untouched.
> A Roam-origin reference with a `FileReference` row is resolved through that row, not passed through.

**Notes** — replace the Roam-origin bullet:
> Pass-through is the no-row case, not the Roam-origin case. Genuinely external links have no row; so does an asset whose bytes could not be copied at publish, which is the documented degradation. A Roam-origin URL that *does* have a row is resolved like any other. See [Decision 2](https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/TpIHc4zeb).

## ENG-2219

**Notes** — add:
> The stage is origin-agnostic: it iterates the node's `FileReference` rows, not its markdown's link shapes.

Its Done When still says "An **Obsidian-origin** node with an image imports into Roam" — I'd leave that as the headline scenario but add:
> A Roam-origin node with an image imports into a second Roam graph, and the image renders from that graph's own storage.

---

Two flags before any of this goes to Linear:

- **ENG-1870 is still the furthest off** and now underpins everything — its Solution is one line about *detecting* references, where the design has it fetch, hash, upload, and write rows.
- **The `filename` column and disambiguation have no ticket at all**, and the migration plan says disambiguation must ship *with* ENG-1870, not after.

Want those two drafted before I write any of it?

content: We're reworking the cross-app assets design after the pivot to copying Roam assets into Supabase; design.md is updated and I've drafted Linear revisions for ENG-1872, ENG-2217, and ENG-2219. Next: say whether to also draft ENG-1870 and the filename-column ticket before writing to Linear.

content.text: Roam graph: discourse-graphs { "uid": "8Sw0uS60r", "title": "(block — not a page)", "content": "- See proposal.md — Why, for motivation. The constraints that shape the approach: - **Obsidian assets are content-addressed and private.** `addFile` (`packages/database/src/lib/files.ts`) hashes the bytes with SHA-256, uploads them to the `assets` bucket under the hash as object name, and inserts a `FileReference` row. The bucket is not public: `storage_select_assets_access` (`supabase/schemas/assets.sql`) requires an authenticated user who passes `file_access(name)`. A browser `` tag cannot fetch these bytes. - **Roam assets are world-readable and not ours.** All 1,932 Firebase URLs in the graph export share one bucket, `firescript-577a2.appspot.com` — Roam's own Firebase project — with the path shape `imgs/app//<10-char random name>.` and a Firebase download token on 100% of them. - **Roam's upload API gives us no control over the URL.** We choose neither bucket nor path: the stored object name is a fresh random uid on every call, so the URL of an already-uploaded file cannot be derived or predicted. - **`file.upload` returns a block string, not a URL**, and its shape depends on the media type: `![](url)` for images, `{{[[pdf]]: url}}` / `{{[[audio]]: url}}` / `{{[[video]]: url}}` for those, and a bare URL for everything else. The mirror has to unwrap it to get the URL for the registry, and it means a non-image asset should be embedded with Roam's own syntax rather than the markdown `![]()` the source note used. (`roamAlphaAPI.util.uploadFile` is a legacy alias for the same call.) - **The original filename is preserved, in Firebase custom metadata.** Verified against a real upload: requesting the Storage URL with `alt=media` **stripped** returns the object descriptor as JSON, and the uploaded name is in `metadata["file-name"]` (alongside `metadata["file-type"]`): - ```javascript "contentDisposition": "inline; filename*=utf-8''lqp2ioVNC3.png", "md5Hash": "REDACTED", "metadata": { "file-type": "image/png", "file-name": "CleanShot 2025-11-16 at 17.14.44@2x.png" }``` - Three consequences. It is how the publisher fills `filename` (Decision 8), at publish time, once per asset — rather than every destination doing it per import. The read is **cheap** — a small JSON response, no bytes — which is what makes Decision 4's recovery path viable, and it bypasses the Roam API entirely. And it is invisible to `curl -I`: `contentDisposition` echoes only the storage uid, so a HEAD on the content URL yields a false negative. The descriptor also carries `md5Hash`, a content fingerprint available without downloading. - **The Roam API itself has no metadata-only read.** `file.get({url})` resolves to a `File`; with `format: "base64"`, to `{base64, filename, mimetype}`. Both transfer the content. `get` restores the name by reading `metadata["file-name"]`; where that key is absent it falls back to the storage uid, which is why Roam's own reference example shows `File {name: "GVfB6XBcMR.pdf", …}`. - `file.delete({url})` is the third operation available. - **Roam never collects uploaded files, and says so.** Its documentation: "Deleting a block doesn't delete the file that was uploaded in it. The upload stays in your graph's storage… There's no way to search for those leftover files yet." Checked all six sections against the local file. Context, Goals, D4, D5, D6, D7, D8 and the new Risks bullets all mirrored correctly. Seven misses, four of which leave the doc contradicting itself.

**The three decision headings weren't updated** — only their bodies were. Each now asserts the opposite of what it contains:

| Roam heading (current) | should be |
|---|---|
| 1. Find assets by parsing markdown; **store no asset index** | 1. Find assets by parsing markdown; **add only the column a consumer reads** |
| 2. Roam-origin assets **stay on Firebase** | 2. Roam-origin assets **are copied into Supabase; the markdown is not rewritten** |
| 3. Mirror **Obsidian-origin** assets to Firebase, choosing durability over revocability | 3. **Mirror assets into Firebase on import**, choosing durability over revocability |

D2's is the worst — the heading says assets stay on Firebase, the first bullet says we copy them to Supabase.

**D2's "Why the URL stays in the markdown" bullet is still the pre-agnosticism text.** It sits two bullets above "A destination resolves by row, never by origin," and contradicts it — it still justifies keeping the URL on the grounds that Roam-to-Roam pass-through needs it. Replacement:

> **Why the URL stays in the markdown:** it is the token the source page contains, exactly as a vault path is the token an Obsidian note contains. Keeping it is what lets it serve as the `FileReference` primary-key component and as the importer's `pathMapping` key (`importNodes.ts:835`). It is also the degradation path: when bytes cannot be copied no row is written, and the URL in the markdown is all a destination has.

**Migration Plan step 2 is stale and now false.** It reads "Land Roam-origin detection and reporting (Decision 2) and the Obsidian validations. Both are read-only with respect to assets." Publish now writes bytes and rows. Replacement:

> 2. Land Roam-origin publication (Decision 2): fetch, hash, upload, write the row. Land the importer's `filename` rule and filename disambiguation alongside it, not after — Roam's flat namespace is what makes disambiguation necessary, so the two arrive together or the first one corrupts vaults.

The section's intro and rollback *were* updated, so it's half-current. Step 3 also lost its `3.` numbering.

**Open Questions bullet 2** still reads "What size cap should the **mirror** apply?" → "What size cap should **each direction** apply?" (the matching Risks bullet was updated).

Cosmetic, from pasting: D2 bullets 1, 2 and 4 and the Risks size-cap bullet begin `- -`; D4 has `namespace .`; D7 has a stray blank line before "What would be worth a field".

content.text:
Grounded. Two findings that shape the split:

**`addFile` already does most of the publish-side work.** It hashes, checks `file_exists`, uploads to the bucket, inserts the `FileReference`, and handles duplicate-key by updating. So Roam publish doesn't reimplement any of that — it needs to *fetch from Firebase* and call `addFile`. That's also why this direction needs no registry: `file_exists` is the dedup, which is exactly D4's asymmetry made concrete.

**But `addFile` takes `fname`, not `filename`.** Adding the column changes its signature, in `packages/database`, which Obsidian's publisher also calls. That ripple isn't costed anywhere yet.

**And the FK forces an ordering:** `FileReference` → `Content`, so the asset stage must run *after* `upsert_content`, not alongside it.

## The seams

```
[1] filename column + addFile signature      packages/database   blocks 2,3,4
     |
     +-- [2] Obsidian: use filename, disambiguate    apps/obsidian
     |
     +-- [3] Fetch one Firebase asset -> addFile     apps/roam
              |
              +-- [4] Asset publication stage        apps/roam
                      after upsert_content
```

Compare to the import side: ENG-1872 needed four pieces because `file.upload` isn't idempotent (registry) and destination URLs change (link rewriter). Publish needs neither — Supabase dedups by hash for free, and D2 doesn't rewrite the markdown. **So this direction is genuinely smaller**, and mirroring ENG-1872's four-way split would be cargo-culting the shape.

## Where each piece goes

**[1] its own ticket, not folded into ENG-1864.** ENG-1864 is types, fixtures and documentation and is already Todo; a migration plus a shared-signature change is different work with a different blast radius. It blocks everything else here, so it wants to be visible on its own.

**[2] its own ticket.** Different app, different direction — it isn't ENG-1870 work. But per the migration plan it must *ship with* [4], not merely before it: publication landing first is what corrupts vaults. That's a `related` link plus an explicit note, since Linear's `blocks` doesn't express "must not ship without."

**[3] and [4] are the real question.** Two options:

- **Split, mirroring ENG-2218/ENG-2219.** [3] is unit-testable against a fixture URL with no publish path; [4] is the integration. Consistent with the other direction.

Drafts only — nothing written to Linear.

## Ticket A

**Title:** Add a `filename` column to `FileReference`

### Problem

- A Roam-origin `FileReference` carries a Firebase URL in `filepath`, which contains no filename.
- A destination needing a name would otherwise have to recognise a Firebase URL and read Roam's custom metadata — provenance detection in the consumer, which the shared contract exists to prevent.

### Solution

- Add `filename` to `FileReference`: nullable, not part of the primary key.
- Add a `filename` parameter to `addFile` (`packages/database/src/lib/files.ts`), threaded into both the insert and the duplicate-key update.
- Regenerate `dbTypes.ts`.

### Done When

- A row can be written with or without `filename`, and existing callers still compile.
- Re-publishing a node whose asset name changed updates `filename` rather than leaving the old one.
- The GC triggers, `file_access`, and the bucket policy are untouched.

### Out of Scope

- Renaming `filepath` to `path_or_url`. Post-v0, together with any further asset columns.
- Making `filehash` nullable. Explicitly rejected — `after_delete_update_fref` would send `NULL` into `file_gc` and fail the delete.
- Backfilling existing rows. All are Obsidian-origin and carry a vault path a name is derivable from.

### Notes

- [Decision 8](https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/kd6Wpn_VF).
- `addFile`'s duplicate-key path updates on `(source_local_id, space_id, filepath)`. `filename` must be included there, or a re-publish silently keeps a stale name.
- Blocks ENG-1870 and Ticket B.

---

## Ticket B

**Title:** Resolve imported asset names from `filename`, and disambiguate collisions

### Problem

- The importer derives a vault path from `filepath` by splitting on `/` and sanitising each segment (`importNodes.ts:896-901`). A Firebase URL through that becomes a deep nonsense directory.
- On a target-path clash it overwrites under an mtime check, with no suffixing. Roam's asset namespace is flat (`imgs/app/<graph>/<random>`), so imported names carry no uniqueness and many will be `image.png`.

### Solution

- Use `filename` for the vault name when present; otherwise decompose `filepath` as today.
- Suffix a colliding target path, keyed on `filehash` so re-imports stay stable.

### Done When

- A Roam-origin reference with `filename` set imports under a readable name, with no part of the URL in the path.
- Two different assets sharing a `filename` in one space both import, both intact.
- Re-importing an unchanged node neither renames nor duplicates its assets.
- An Obsidian-origin row with `filename` null imports exactly as today.

### Out of Scope

- Any change to how references are found in markdown.

### Notes

- [Decision 8](https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/kd6Wpn_VF), prerequisite clause.
- **Must ship with ENG-1870, not after it.** Publication landing first puts opaque names and silently clobbered files into vaults, and neither is correctable later — renaming breaks links users wrote themselves.
- The same suffixing incidentally closes an existing narrow case: `getAssetPathRelativeToNote` can relativize two distinct vault paths to the same leaf, which collides today.
- Blocked by Ticket A.

- **Labels.** B is clearly `Obsidian plugin`. A touches `packages/database` and both apps — `Share and publish`, or no app label? I'd rather not guess.
- **"Must ship with"** has no Linear relation that expresses it. I'd use `related` between B and ENG-1870 plus the note, since `blocks` would wrongly imply B must land first.

ENG-1870's own rewrite is still outstanding — it's the reverted original, one line about detecting references. Say the word and I'll draft it to match.

content.text:
## ENG-1870 (rewrite, kept whole)

**Proposed title:** `Detect and report asset references in Roam-origin shared nodes` → **`Copy Roam-origin assets into Supabase on publish`**

### Problem

- Roam shared-node markdown references files held in Roam's Firebase storage. Nothing puts those bytes where a destination can resolve them the ordinary way, so every destination would have to know about Firebase to use them.
- An asset that cannot be copied must not stop the node from publishing.

### Solution

- After content upsert, find the asset references in the node's `full` markdown, fetch each from Firebase, and pass it to `addFile` with its original filename.
- Leave the markdown unchanged. The Firebase URL stays as the reference token and becomes the row's `filepath`.
- Skip an asset over an explicit size limit, and return failures as part of the publish result.

### Done When

- Publishing a Roam node with an image writes a `FileReference` whose `filepath` is the URL as it appears in the markdown and whose `filename` is the original upload name.
- The published markdown is unchanged by the asset stage.
- An asset that cannot be fetched does not fail the publish, and appears in the result.
- Re-publishing an unchanged node uploads no bytes again.

### Out of Scope

- Rewriting asset links in published markdown. [Decision 2](https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/TpIHc4zeb) keeps the URL as the reference token.
- Destination-side import. ENG-1872 and its sub-issues cover that.
- Garbage collection of copied bytes. The existing `file_gc` path already handles it.
- Backfilling nodes already published from Roam. Their markdown still holds working URLs; a worklist is derivable from `Content.text` when wanted.

### Notes

- [Decision 2](https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/TpIHc4zeb).
- **Ordering:** `FileReference` has a foreign key to `Content`, so this stage runs after `upsert_content`, not alongside it.
- `addFile` already hashes, dedups through `file_exists`, uploads, and resolves duplicate keys. This ticket fetches from Firebase and calls it — it reimplements none of that, and needs no registry, because Supabase deduplicates by hash on its own.
- The original filename comes from the Firebase object descriptor: request the storage URL with `alt=media` stripped and read `metadata["file-name"]`. Fall back to the storage uid where that key is absent, as Roam's own `file.get` does.
- Set the size limit in this ticket. It is a different limit from the import side's — what we are willing to pull out of Firebase and store at our cost, not what Roam will accept.
- The reverted criterion "persisted with the node's access scope" holds by construction: a `FileReference` hangs off the node's `Content` row, so it is reachable exactly when the node is. See [Decision 7](https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/xlPuc0A6E).
- **Not split**, unlike ENG-1872. That direction needed a registry because `file.upload` is not idempotent, and a link rewriter because destination URLs change. Neither applies here.
- Blocked by Ticket A. Must ship with Ticket B.

---

That's all three drafted. The dependency picture they form:

```
Ticket A  filename column + addFile
   |
   +--> ENG-1870  copy on publish  <--ship together--> Ticket B  Obsidian names
   |
   +--> ENG-2216 ... ENG-2219  (import side, unchanged)
```

Ticket A is now the single unblocked root for both directions — it displaces ENG-2216 as the thing someone could start today.

Still open before any of this is written: the **label** question on Ticket A, and whether ENG-1870 stays Backlog or moves to Todo with the rest.

input.title: Copy Roam-origin assets into Supabase on publish
input.description:
## Problem

- Roam shared-node markdown references files held in Roam's Firebase storage. Nothing puts those bytes where a destination can resolve them the ordinary way, so every destination would have to know about Firebase to use them.
- An asset that cannot be copied must not stop the node from publishing.

## Solution

- After content upsert, find the asset references in the node's `full` markdown, fetch each from Firebase, and pass it to `addFile` with its original filename.
- Leave the markdown unchanged. The Firebase URL stays as the reference token and becomes the row's `filepath`.
- Skip an asset over an explicit size limit, and return failures as part of the publish result.

## Done When

- Publishing a Roam node with an image writes a `FileReference` whose `filepath` is the URL as it appears in the markdown and whose `filename` is the original upload name.
- The published markdown is unchanged by the asset stage.
- An asset that cannot be fetched does not fail the publish, and appears in the result.
- Re-publishing an unchanged node uploads no bytes again.

## Out of Scope

- Rewriting asset links in published markdown. Decision 2 keeps the URL as the reference token.
- Destination-side import. ENG-1872 and its sub-issues cover that.
- Garbage collection of copied bytes. The existing `file_gc` path already handles it.
- Backfilling nodes already published from Roam. Their markdown still holds working URLs, and a worklist is derivable from `Content.text` when one is wanted.

## Notes

- [Decision 2](https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/TpIHc4zeb) on [OpenSpec/CrossApp asset references](https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/Ex0HuOqBS).
- **Ordering:** `FileReference` has a foreign key to `Content`, so this stage runs after `upsert_content`, not alongside it.
- `addFile` already hashes, deduplicates through `file_exists`, uploads, and resolves duplicate keys. This ticket fetches from Firebase and calls it — it reimplements none of that, and needs no registry, because Supabase deduplicates by hash on its own.
- The original filename comes from the Firebase object descriptor: request the storage URL with `alt=media` stripped and read `metadata["file-name"]`. Fall back to the storage uid where that key is absent, as Roam's own `file.get` does.
- Set the size limit in this ticket. It is a different limit from the import side's — what we are willing to pull out of Firebase and store at our cost, not what Roam will accept.
- The earlier criterion "persisted with the node's access scope" holds by construction: a `FileReference` hangs off the node's `Content` row, so it is reachable exactly when the node is. See [Decision 7](https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/xlPuc0A6E).
- **Not split**, unlike ENG-1872. That direction needed a registry because `file.upload` is not idempotent, and a link rewriter because destination URLs change. Neither applies here.
- Functional requirement F10.

message.content: Ok. Let's started on the specs. Give me the top-level of what you expect to see there, because I still need to understand better what you expect there.

content.text:
The distinction that makes this answerable: **a ticket says what to build and then closes; a requirement says what must stay true forever.** So the filter isn't "is it important" — it's "would a future change that broke this be a bug?" That's also why ENG-2216's registry contributes nothing here: replace the registry with something else and no user or plugin can tell.

`specs/cross-app-assets/spec.md`, one file, opening with a `## Purpose` since it's a new capability — and the repo's first main spec, so that Purpose survives into `openspec/specs/` after archive.

## Proposed requirements

| # | Requirement | What's observable |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **A published node carries its assets** | After publish, each asset the node references has its bytes in shared storage and a reference recorded against that node |
| 2 | **Publication does not rewrite the source's asset references** | The reference token in published content is exactly the token the source contained |
| 3 | **A destination resolves assets by reference, not by origin** | Same import behavior regardless of which host published — including a host importing content it originally published |
| 4 | **An unresolvable asset degrades to its original reference** | No stored bytes → the token is left untouched and still renders if it can |
| 5 | **An asset failure never fails the node** | Node publishes/imports intact; the failure is reported |
| 6 | **Imported assets get stable, non-colliding local names** | Readable names, two same-named assets both survive, re-import doesn't rename or duplicate |
| 7 | **An asset is exactly as visible as the node referencing it** | No separate asset permission to get wrong |
| 8 | **Repeated syncs do not duplicate stored bytes** | One asset referenced twice is stored once; re-sync grows storage by nothing |

Roughly 20 scenarios across those — comparable to `add-client-version-channel` (153 lines, similar count).

## What's deliberately *not* in it

Everything that could change without a consumer noticing: the registry and where it lives, `addFile`, the `filename` column and `filepath` semantics, Firebase descriptor reads, `imgs/app/<graph>/…`, the `file_gc` triggers, the round-trip mechanics. Those are design and tasks material. **#7 is the interesting case** — it's a real requirement, but the *reason* it holds (a `FileReference` hangs off the node's `Content` row) is design. The spec states the guarantee; D7 explains why we get it for free.

Note #3 and #8 are where the design's hardest-won decisions surface as behavior — #3 is the origin-agnosticism you pushed me on, #8 is what D4 exists to deliver — but neither names a mechanism.

## Two register questions before I draft

**How host-neutral?** I'd write requirements in terms of "a source host" and "a destination host", with scenarios that name Roam and Obsidian concretely — because the sharp cases only exist named ("Roam imports a Roam-origin node and stores its own copy"). The alternative is naming hosts throughout, which reads more plainly but bakes two hosts into a contract meant to admit a third.

**Does the size cap belong?** I have it as a scenario under #4 ("over the configured limit → degrades"), with no number. It's still an open question in the design, and stating it as *behavior at a threshold* lets the spec be written before the number is chosen. Alternative is leaving caps out entirely as a policy detail.

Does that shape match what you expected, or is it broader/narrower than you had in mind?

input.content:
## Purpose

Lets a node published from one platform carry the images and attachments its content references to another platform, so a reader on the destination sees the same content rather than broken links, and so neither platform needs to know which platform an asset originally came from.

## ADDED Requirements

### Requirement: A published node carries its assets

When a source platform publishes a node, the system SHALL store the bytes of each asset that node's content references, and SHALL record a reference associating those bytes with that node.

#### Scenario: Node referencing an image is published

- **WHEN** a platform publishes a node whose content embeds an image held in that platform's own storage
- **THEN** the image's bytes are stored in shared storage, and a reference associating them with the node is recorded

#### Scenario: Node referencing no assets is published

- **WHEN** a platform publishes a node whose content references no assets
- **THEN** the node publishes and no asset references are recorded for it

#### Scenario: Node is republished after an asset is added

- **WHEN** a node that has already been published gains a new asset reference and is published again
- **THEN** a reference is recorded for the new asset, and the references already recorded for that node remain valid

### Requirement: Publication does not rewrite the source's asset references

Published content SHALL express each asset reference exactly as the source platform's content expressed it. The system SHALL NOT substitute a different token when publishing.

#### Scenario: Source expresses a reference as a URL

- **WHEN** a platform whose content addresses assets by URL publishes a node embedding one
- **THEN** the published content carries that URL unchanged

#### Scenario: Source expresses a reference as a file path

- **WHEN** a platform whose content addresses assets by path publishes a note embedding one
- **THEN** the published content carries that path unchanged

### Requirement: A destination resolves assets by reference, not by origin

A destination platform SHALL resolve an asset by looking up the reference recorded against the node and retrieving the stored bytes. It SHALL NOT vary that behavior according to which platform published the node, and SHALL NOT inspect a reference token to infer where the asset came from.

#### Scenario: Destination imports a node published by a different platform

- **WHEN** a platform imports a node published by another platform, and that node has a recorded asset reference
- **THEN** the asset is retrieved through the recorded reference and rendered from the destination's own copy

#### Scenario: Destination imports a node its own platform published

- **WHEN** a platform imports a node originally published from that same platform, whose reference token that platform could follow directly
- **THEN** the asset is still retrieved through the recorded reference and stored as the destination's own copy, rather than left pointing at the origin's storage

#### Scenario: Two destinations import the same node

- **WHEN** two different platforms import the same published node
- **THEN** each resolves the asset by the same rule, and neither requires knowledge of the publishing platform's storage

Valid on `--strict`. `specs` → **done**, `tasks` → **ready**.

`specs/cross-app-assets/spec.md` — 8 requirements, 25 scenarios, all in platform terms.

Three judgment calls worth challenging:

**1. I gave requirement 7 a scenario about what we *don't* control.** "Reference token is independently retrievable" says a public source URL stays publicly retrievable, and that the requirement governs only the bytes in shared storage. That's unusual — a scenario asserting a limit rather than a guarantee — but the alternative is a spec that reads as though publishing confers access control it doesn't. D7 makes the same point ("unenforceable, since we cannot change the readability of someone else's bucket"). If it reads as scope-creep, it's the first thing to cut.

**2. "SHALL NOT inspect a reference token to infer where the asset came from"** is close to prescribing implementation — arguably a destination could sniff origin and still behave identically. I kept it because origin-agnosticism is the property you pushed me on, and it's only testable as a prohibition. But it's the one clause that fails the "could the implementation change without a consumer noticing" test.

**3. The size cap is a threshold with no number** — "larger than the configured limit for that transfer." Lets the spec stand while the number is still an open question, and "for that transfer" leaves room for the two directions having different caps.

What I deliberately left out, in case any of these were expected: `filename`, `filepath`, `FileReference` by name, the registry, Firebase, Supabase, the round-trip mechanics, `file_gc`. The spec names no storage system and no plugin API.

For `tasks.md`, the instruction gates on design Open Questions — "resolve them with the user first, do not bake an unstated assumption into the task list." Of the three:

| | blocks tasks? |
|---|---|
| How to surface skipped assets | No — ENG-1877 owns presentation |
| **What size cap each direction applies** | Needs a task saying *choose it*, and what governs the choice |
| What triggers a deletion pass | No — design says nothing needs to know now |

So tasks is writable, with the cap appearing as a decision task rather than a number. Want me to go ahead?

### Requirement: An asset failure never fails the node

Publishing and importing a node SHALL complete even when one or more of its assets cannot be handled, and the system SHALL report each asset that could not be handled.

#### Scenario: An asset cannot be retrieved during publication

- **WHEN** a node is published and one of its assets cannot be read from the source platform's storage
- **THEN** the node publishes with its content intact, and the failed asset appears in the result

#### Scenario: An asset cannot be retrieved during import

- **WHEN** a node is imported and one of its recorded assets cannot be retrieved from shared storage
- **THEN** the node imports with its content intact, and the failed asset appears in the result

#### Scenario: Every asset on a node fails

- **WHEN** a node is published or imported and none of its assets can be handled
- **THEN** the node is still published or imported, and every failure is reported

### Requirement: Imported assets get stable, non-colliding local names

Where a destination materializes asset bytes into its own storage, it SHALL derive a local name from what the reference records, SHALL NOT overwrite a distinct asset already held under that name, and SHALL produce the same result when the same node is imported again.

#### Scenario: Reference records an original name

- **WHEN** a destination materializes an asset whose reference records the name it was originally stored under
- **THEN** the local name is derived from that recorded name, and no part of the reference token appears in it

#### Scenario: Two distinct assets share a recorded name

- **WHEN** a destination materializes two assets with different content whose references record the same name
- **THEN** both are materialized under distinct local names, and neither replaces the other

#### Scenario: Unchanged node is imported again

- **WHEN** a node whose assets have not changed is imported a second time
- **THEN** no asset is renamed, duplicated, or re-materialized

#### Scenario: Reference records no original name

- **WHEN** a destination materializes an asset whose reference records no name
- **THEN** a local name is derived deterministically from the reference itself, and repeated imports produce the same name

### Requirement: An asset is exactly as visible as the node referencing it

Read access to stored asset bytes SHALL be determined by read access to the node that references them. The system SHALL NOT carry a separate per-asset permission.

#### Scenario: Reader can access the node

- **WHEN** a reader who can read a published node requests one of its stored assets
- **THEN** the bytes are returned

#### Scenario: Reader cannot access the node

- **WHEN** a reader who cannot read a published node requests one of its stored assets
- **THEN** the request is refused

#### Scenario: Access to the node is withdrawn

- **WHEN** a reader's access to a node is withdrawn and they request one of its stored assets
- **THEN** the request is refused, without any per-asset change

- **WHEN** an asset's reference token is one that can be retrieved without the system's authorization, such as a public URL held by the source platform

#### Scenario: Two nodes reference identical content

- **WHEN** two published nodes reference assets whose content is identical
- **THEN** one copy of the bytes is stored, with a reference recorded for each node

#### Scenario: Unchanged node is published again

- **WHEN** a node whose assets have not changed is published a second time
- **THEN** no additional asset bytes are stored

#### Scenario: Node already holding an asset imports another referencing it

content.text:
Two changes are mechanical; one is a real question I'd rather put to you than decide.

## The mechanical part

**Solution** — bullet 1 still lists fields that were designed out:

> ~~Define shared asset metadata for source reference, downloadable bytes, MIME/type, size, access scope, and fallback status.~~
> A reference is a `FileReference` row: the token exactly as the node's content expresses it, the content hash, and an optional original name. Nothing else.

Bullet 3 ("Document missing, oversized, unsupported, and URL-only behaviors") is now done by `specs/cross-app-assets/spec.md` — point at it rather than restating, or the two drift.

**Done When** — "Fixtures cover a downloadable asset and a **URL-only asset fallback**" can't be satisfied as written. A URL-only asset has **no row** (`filehash` is `NOT NULL`), so there's no `FileReference` fixture to write. The fixture is a *content* fixture: markdown carrying a token with no row behind it. Small wording change, but it's the difference between a fixture that can exist and one that can't.

**Notes** — my addition currently reads as a list of removals. It should record the one field that earned its way in:

> `filename` was added for the opposite reason: it is the one piece a destination cannot derive, and without it an importer would have to detect a Firebase URL and read Roam's custom metadata — provenance detection in the consumer ([Decision 8](https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/kd6Wpn_VF)).

**Blocker** — ENG-1864 should be `blockedBy` ENG-2229. Its fixtures need the `filename` column to exist; that's tasks 1.1–1.2 before 1.3.

## The real question

The proposal's Impact section still says:

> New `CrossAppAsset` type; `CrossAppNode` gains an optional `assets` field.

**Does anything read that field?** Obsidian's importer already fetches references by node id (`fetchFileReferences`, `importNodes.ts:452-472`), and Roam's importer would do the same. If both destinations query the rows, an `assets` array on the node payload has no consumer — which is exactly the test that removed `accessScope`, MIME type and size.

If that's right, ENG-1864 shrinks to: *the reference is the row shape, plus fixtures* — and "define a payload type" comes off, with a line in Out of Scope saying destinations query recorded references rather than reading an embedded list. The proposal would need the matching edit.

If instead you want the node payload to carry assets — say, so a destination can see what it's about to fetch before fetching, or so the contract doesn't presume database access — then the type stays and ENG-1864 keeps its original shape.

I lean toward removing it, on the same no-reader grounds as the rest. But it's the one place where "the contract" could reasonably mean a payload rather than a table, and that's a call about what the contract *is*, not a cleanup.

`SharedNode` is a thin descriptor; content is fetched separately by view query. So the Roam importer reads assets by adding a `my_file_references` query **exactly parallel to Obsidian's** — same view, same key, same RLS.

Which answers the contract question: **the contract is the view, not a type.** `my_file_references` already *is* the shared, RLS-scoped shape both apps read — and it's also the mechanism behind spec requirement 7, since its `WHERE` bottoms out in `my_space_ids('reader')` and `my_accessible_resources()`. An `assets` array on the node payload would be a second copy of it with no reader.

## And that surfaces a real gap in ENG-2229

The view has an **explicit column list**:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW public.my_file_references AS
SELECT source_local_id, space_id, filepath, filehash, created, last_modified
FROM public."FileReference" ...
```

Adding `filename` to the table does **not** surface it in the view. Both importers read the view, not the table. So as ENG-2229 is currently written — table column, `addFile`, `dbTypes` — `filename` would be invisible to every consumer, and the ticket would pass its own Done When while delivering nothing.

ENG-2229 needs:

- **Solution:** add `filename` to the `my_file_references` select list.
- **Done When:** a row written with a `filename` is visible through `my_file_references` with that value, read as a non-privileged user.

That last one is the criterion that actually proves the feature works end to end.

So the ENG-1864 revision becomes: contract = the view's shape (token, hash, name, timestamps), plus fixtures, plus the no-row degradation case — and `CrossAppAsset` comes off, along with the proposal's Impact line naming it.

Want me to draft both ticket updates plus the proposal edit?

{"id":"ENG-2229","uuid":"bf853951-4407-4c8f-b22a-95e32c9f14ea","title":"Add a `filename` column to FileReference","description":"## Problem

* A Roam-origin `FileReference` carries a Firebase URL in `filepath`, which contains no filename.
* A destination needing a name would otherwise have to recognise a Firebase URL and read Roam's custom metadata — provenance detection in the consumer, which the shared contract exists to prevent.

## Solution

* Add `filename` to `FileReference`: nullable, not part of the primary key.
* Add `filename` to the `my_file_references` select list. The view has an explicit column list, so a new column on the table is otherwise invisible to every consumer.
* Add a `filename` parameter to `addFile` (`packages/database/src/lib/files.ts`), threaded into both the insert and the duplicate-key update.
* Regenerate `dbTypes.ts`.

## Done When

* A row can be written with or without `filename`, and existing callers still compile.
* A row written with a `filename` is visible through `my_file_references` with that value, read as a non-privileged user. Both importers read the view rather than the table, so this is what proves the column reaches a consumer.
* Re-publishing a node whose asset name changed updates `filename` rather than leaving the old one.
* The garbage-collection triggers, `file_access`, and the bucket policy are untouched.

## Out of Scope

* Renaming `filepath` to `path_or_url`. Post-v0, together with any further asset columns.
* Making `filehash` nullable. Explicitly rejected — `after_delete_update_fref` would send `NULL` into `file_gc` and fail the delete outright.

{"id":"ENG-1864","uuid":"ca579c26-4be5-4a26-9cfe-bd5375ecdb5a","title":"Define cross-app asset reference contract","description":"## Problem

* Roam and Obsidian need a shared asset reference shape for markdown import and link preservation.
* MVP0 must handle downloadable assets and URL-only fallbacks without blocking node sharing.

## Solution

* Define the reference shape: the token exactly as the node's content expresses it, the content hash, and an optional original name. Nothing else.
* Add Roam-origin and Obsidian-origin asset fixtures tied to shared node markdown, including a node whose content carries a token with no stored asset behind it.
* Support the missing, oversized, unsupported and no-row behaviors. These are specified as scenarios in the change's `cross-app-assets` spec; the work here is to make the shape carry them, not to restate them.

## Done When

* Shared asset reference payloads are documented or typed.
* Fixtures cover a stored asset and a node whose content carries a token with no stored asset behind it. The second is a content fixture rather than a reference fixture: `filehash` is `NOT NULL`, so an asset whose bytes were never stored has no row at all.
* Follow-up asset tickets can reference this contract without redefining payload shape.

## Out of Scope

* Uploading or downloading asset bytes.
* Markdown link rewriting in either app.
* Asset refresh behavior beyond metadata shape.

## Notes

* Functional requirements: [F10: Source asset publication](<https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/D-7HqQmKp>), [F11: Destination asset import and link rewrite](<https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/j3AqDVwfU>).
* Depends on [ENG-1847](<https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/issue/ENG-1847/define-shared-cross-app-node-content-contract>).
* Keep the contract source-neutral; app-specific asset handling belongs in implementation tickets.
* Two items from the original solution were designed out. `accessScope` was dropped because row-level security on the referencing node already determines read access, so a per-asset field would duplicate it more weakly ([Decision 7](<https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/xlPuc0A6E>)). Stored MIME type and size were dropped because no consumer reads them, and both are available from storage metadata when needed ([Decision 1](<https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/GQtp4l7g1>)).
* `filename` was added for the opposite reason to the fields above. It is the one piece a destination cannot derive for itself: without it an importer would have to recognise a Firebase URL and read Roam's own custom metadata, which is provenance detection in the consumer ([Decision 8](<https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/kd6Wpn_VF>)). content.text:
ENG-1864 updated — Solution rewritten, the impossible fixture criterion fixed, the `filename` counterpoint added to Notes, and `blockedBy: ENG-2229` set.

Everything I changed is neutral on the `CrossAppNode.assets` question. The new Solution bullet 1 says what a reference *carries* without saying where it lives, so it reads correctly whether the contract turns out to be the view alone or the view plus a payload type.

Three things I left untouched because they *do* depend on that decision:

* Roam and Obsidian need a shared asset reference shape for markdown import and link preservation.
* MVP0 must handle downloadable assets and URL-only fallbacks without blocking node sharing.

## Solution

* Define the reference shape: the token exactly as the node's content expresses it, the content hash, and an optional original name. Nothing else.
* Add Roam-origin and Obsidian-origin asset fixtures tied to shared node markdown, including a node whose content carries a token with no stored asset behind it.
* Support the missing, oversized, unsupported and no-row behaviors. These are specified as scenarios in the change's `cross-app-assets` spec; the work here is to make the shape carry them, not to restate them.

## Done When

* Shared asset reference payloads are documented or typed.
* Fixtures cover a stored asset and a node whose content carries a token with no stored asset behind it. The second is a content fixture rather than a reference fixture: `filehash` is `NOT NULL`, so an asset whose bytes were never stored has no row at all.
* Follow-up asset tickets can reference this contract without redefining payload shape.

## Out of Scope

* Uploading or downloading asset bytes.
* Markdown link rewriting in either app.
* Asset refresh behavior beyond metadata shape.

## Notes

* Functional requirements: [F10: Source asset publication](<https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/D-7HqQmKp>), [F11: Destination asset import and link rewrite](<https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/j3AqDVwfU>).
* Depends on [ENG-1847](<https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/issue/ENG-1847/define-shared-cross-app-node-content-contract>).
* Keep the contract source-neutral; app-specific asset handling belongs in implementation tickets.
* Two items from the original solution were designed out. `accessScope` was dropped because row-level security on the referencing node already determines read access, so a per-asset field would duplicate it more weakly ([Decision 7](<https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/xlPuc0A6E>)). Stored MIME type and size were dropped because no consumer reads them, and both are available from storage metadata when needed ([Decision 1](<https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/GQtp4l7g1>)).
* `filename` was added for the opposite reason to the fields above. It is the one piece a destination cannot derive for itself: without it an importer would have to recognise a Firebase URL and read Roam's own custom metadata, which is provenance detection in the consumer ([Decision 8](<https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/kd6Wpn_VF>)). The column itself is added by <issue id="bf853951-4407-4c8f-b22a-95e32c9f14ea" href="https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/issue/ENG-2229/add-a-filename-column-to-filereference">ENG-2229</issue>.
* `CrossAppNode.assets` is defined here but has no runtime producer yet. `dbToCrossAppConverters` has no `CrossAppNode` converter — reads still go through the historical `SharedNode`. When that converter is written it should run the `my_file_references` query and populate `assets`.
